memoryText: Oh, taste and see that the LORD is good! Blessed is the man who takes refuge in him!
readingInstruction: No new reading today. Read Psalm 34:8 slowly, several times, and then say it from memory. Read the meditation and the week in review, and choose one of the three questions to write about, pray over, or share with someone.
memoryVerseMeditation:
This verse is an invitation, not a command to believe on faith alone. David says, in effect, “Try it for yourself.”

“Taste.” You cannot know the flavor of food by reading about it. Tasting is personal and immediate. David is saying that the goodness of God is not only a doctrine. It is something we can experience. He had tasted it in the cave, in Gath, and in the wilderness. He asks us to do the same.

“And see.” The tasting leads to seeing. What the Lord does is visible in the lives of those who trust him. This is the evidence David offers: not a philosophical argument, but a life.

“That the LORD is good.” The goodness of God is the foundation of everything. He is not only powerful, or just, or wise, but good. When we are tempted to doubt, this is the claim we need most. God’s goodness is not diminished by suffering. David wrote this psalm in a time of fear and embarrassment.

“Blessed is the man who takes refuge in him.” The result of tasting is taking shelter. A person who knows that God is good will run to him. The word “blessed” echoes Psalm 1:1 and shows how David’s psalms continue the same theme.

Peter echoes this verse in 1 Peter 2:3: “If indeed you have tasted that the Lord is good.” The Lord is Jesus, and the tasting is personal. At the table of communion, we taste and see in a special way. Throughout the week, ask where you can taste his goodness: in answered prayer, in a kindness, in a beautiful day, in forgiveness.
weekInReview: This week you followed David in the aftermath of his sin. You prayed Psalm 51 with him and saw the pain in his family: Tamar’s suffering, Absalom’s revenge, and the rebellion that drove David from Jerusalem. You saw his humility as he walked out weeping, and how God worked through Hushai. You read the psalms of the wilderness, praising God’s steadfast love as better than life. You saw Absalom’s death and David’s grief, and the king’s restoration. In the appendix of 2 Samuel, David’s song looked back on God’s rescue. In Psalms 34, 56, 57, 30, 35, 38, and 39 you prayed with a man who knew fear, injustice, joy, and mortality. The week taught that God is near to the brokenhearted, that tears are never wasted, and that life is short but his goodness is not.
reflectionQuestions: David told his story of being rescued from a humiliating situation as a song of praise. What embarrassing or hard moment in your life could become a testimony of God’s help?
Psalm 34:18 says the LORD is near to the brokenhearted. How did Jesus, the Man of Sorrows, demonstrate that nearness, and how can you lean on it this week?
Psalm 39 asks God to teach us how brief life is. What would change in how you spend this week if you lived it with that awareness?
prayerPrompts: Taste and see: name one way you have seen God to be good this week.
Thank him for being near to the brokenhearted.
Thank Jesus, who knows your sorrows.
